passage:
I'm Swati, and this is about my friends and me, so don't judge too hard.
There are five of us in the flat. Last month Neha from next door skipped the shared cleaning rota twice, and Sarika said, "Typical. She's so entitled." Everyone agreed. Two weeks later Sarika skipped it three times because of her internship, and the verdict was, "Poor thing, she's swamped." I agreed both times. That's the bit that bugged me.
So one night over instant noodles I said, not accusing, just curious, "Funny, when Neha skipped, she was entitled, and when Sarika skipped, she was busy. Maybe Neha was busy too?"
There was a pause. Sarika went a bit red and said, "Okay. Fair." Then Divya said, "I do this with my brother all the time."
Nobody fought. The next week, someone invited Neha over for chai.

qa.q: How many times did Sarika skip the rota?
qa.a: Three times, because of her internship.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling in the days before speaking up?
qa.a: Swati felt uneasy and a bit guilty, having agreed with two opposite verdicts on the same behaviour.

qa.q: Why did Swati's way of raising it work?
qa.a: It was framed as a curious question, "Maybe Neha was busy too?", so nobody felt accused and they could see the pattern themselves.

qa.q: How might Sarika have felt when Swati pointed out the pattern?
qa.a: Sarika seemed embarrassed, going a bit red, but not attacked, so she could admit "Okay. Fair."

grounding: Shows a student noticing friends judge the same behaviour differently depending on who does it, and naming it gently so they see it themselves.

passage:
Gargi had been on the hiring panel at the Bengaluru office for six months before she saw it. Updating the team sheet one evening, she counted: eight people hired this year, six from Varun's college in Pune. Two had first come in as interns through his alumni group.
It hadn't felt like bias in the room. Varun always said things like, "He'll fit right in," or "We speak the same language." Candidates from his college walked in relaxed, joking about the same canteen. Others, like the woman from a Guwahati college last week, answered carefully and got "good, but not quite a fit."
Gargi scrolled back through her notes. The Guwahati candidate had the highest test score of the month.
At the next panel she said, "Can we score the tests before we discuss fit? Our last eight hires are mostly from one place." Varun blinked, then said slowly, "Huh. That's actually true."

qa.q: How many of the eight hires were from Varun's college?
qa.a: Six from Varun's college in Pune.

qa.q: How did Gargi feel when she saw the Guwahati candidate's test score?
qa.a: Gargi felt troubled and uneasy, realising a strong candidate had been turned away for a vague "fit".

qa.q: Why is scoring tests before discussing fit a useful step?
qa.a: It puts evidence on the table before comfort with the familiar can sway the panel.

qa.q: What might the Guwahati candidate have experienced in that interview?
qa.a: She may have felt like an outsider among in-jokes, answering carefully and leaving unsure why she was "not quite a fit".

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing that hiring keeps favouring people from the manager's own college, where comfort with the familiar passes for merit.

Thursday night.
Dinner at Harman's with the college gang. Loved it, as always: same jokes, same arguments about cricket.
Then Harman started mimicking "those people from the old city" and their accent. Everyone laughed. I laughed at the first line too, out of habit. Then I thought of Wasim from my team, who grew up there, who stayed back two nights last month to fix my broken report.
I said, "Yaar, Wasim talks like that, and he's the sharpest person in our office. Leave it." It came out calmer than I felt. Harman rolled his eyes. "Relax, Baljeet." Then the talk drifted back to cricket. Nobody stayed annoyed for long.
Driving home, I kept wondering what else I've laughed at without noticing. I've asked Wasim to lunch on Saturday. I want to actually hear about his neighbourhood instead of guessing.
I still love that lot. I just don't need anyone to be lesser for us to be close.

qa.q: How many nights did Wasim stay back to fix the report?
qa.a: Two nights last month.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when speaking up at dinner?
qa.a: Baljeet felt more upset inside than it sounded, "calmer than I felt", but steady and still fond of the group.

qa.q: Why is asking Wasim to lunch a good next step for Baljeet?
qa.a: It replaces guesses about the old city with a real person's view, which is how Baljeet can check other assumptions too.

qa.q: How might Harman see Baljeet's comment?
qa.a: Harman seems mildly irritated, rolling his eyes, but not deeply offended, since the evening goes on as usual.

grounding: Shows a young adult checking a habit of laughing along, speaking up calmly when a group is mocked, and seeking other views while staying loyal to friends.

passage:
The class globe lay on the floor with a crack across Africa when Mrs Dutta walked in. "Who did this?"
Silence. Then Rohan said, "Must be Joseph. He's always clumsy."
Swati felt the knot in her stomach loosen. She had bumped that table during the chase game, though she wasn't sure the globe fell then. "Yes, Joseph was near it," she said. Three more voices joined. "Joseph broke the duster last month."
Joseph, small and quiet on the last bench, shook his head and looked at his shoes.
Mrs Dutta looked around. "Who actually saw it fall?" No hands. "Then nobody knows. Joseph, you're not in trouble. We'll all talk about the chase game after lunch."
Swati stared at her desk, face burning.

qa.q: Where was the crack on the class globe?
qa.a: The globe had a crack across Africa.

qa.q: Why did Swati join in blaming Joseph?
qa.a: Swati was afraid of being blamed herself after bumping the table, and pointing at Joseph made that fear ease.

qa.q: What did Mrs Dutta's question "Who actually saw it fall?" achieve?
qa.a: It asked for facts instead of guesses, showed nobody knew, and protected Joseph from the group's blame.

qa.q: What was it like for Joseph when everyone named him?
qa.a: Joseph likely felt helpless and hurt, unable to argue with the whole class, so he just shook his head and looked down.

grounding: Shows children quickly agreeing that one quieter child broke something, which eases their own fear of being blamed.

passage:
At the after-school tuition centre, the whiteboard marker went missing again. Before anyone spoke, Gurleen said, "I didn't take it," and folded her arms. Nobody had asked her.
Hansa didi, the tutor, glanced at her. So did the four others at the table. Gurleen's jaw set. Last week it was the missing sharpener, the week before, the spilled water. Always, "Gurleen, again?"
"Whatever," she muttered. "I'm the bad one anyway." She kicked the table leg, just hard enough to make the pencils jump.
Then Hansa didi found the marker in her own bag. She came and sat beside Gurleen. "It was with me. I'm sorry you had to defend yourself before anyone asked. You're not the bad one."

qa.q: Where did Hansa didi find the marker?
qa.a: In her own bag.

qa.q: Why did Gurleen say "I didn't take it" before anyone asked?
qa.a: Gurleen expected to be blamed as usual, so she felt defensive and hurt even before anyone spoke.

qa.q: What could Hansa didi do next to help Gurleen drop the "bad one" label?
qa.a: Ask what actually happened before looking at anyone, and notice Gurleen's good moments out loud, so the old label stops sticking.

qa.q: How might Hansa didi feel on finding the marker in her own bag?
qa.a: Hansa didi likely felt sorry and a little ashamed, seeing how quickly everyone, including her, had looked at Gurleen.

grounding: Shows a child who has become the default culprit, expects blame and starts to take on the label of the bad one.

"We lost the quiz because Saurabh buzzed too early."
"And the notes didn't get printed because Saurabh forgot the pen drive."
"And the lab slot got cancelled..."
"That was the teacher, Tejas," Meera said.
"Yeah, but Saurabh was supposed to confirm it." Tejas laughed, and the others laughed too. It felt good, somehow, like letting air out of a tyre. Boards were three weeks away and everyone's stomach was in knots.
Saurabh sat at the end of the bench, peeling the label off his water bottle. "I did confirm it. I have the message."
"Sure, bro."
"Can we not do this every day?" Saurabh said quietly.
Nobody answered. Meera looked at Tejas. Tejas looked at his phone. The quiz, the notes, the lab slot: when he thought about it, only the quiz was even partly Saurabh's.

qa.q: How far away were the boards?
qa.a: Boards were three weeks away.

qa.q: Why did blaming Saurabh feel good to Tejas?
qa.a: Tejas was anxious about boards, and laughing at Saurabh let that tension out "like letting air out of a tyre".

qa.q: What could Tejas do now that he sees most of it wasn't Saurabh's fault?
qa.a: Say so to the group, drop the jokes, and check with Saurabh privately; one voice can stop the daily blame.

qa.q: What is it like for Saurabh to hear this every day?
qa.a: Saurabh feels hurt and worn down, carrying the group's exam stress alone, as "Can we not do this every day?" shows.

grounding: Shows a stressed friend group before exams piling every problem onto one member, which relieves their tension while he carries it alone.

passage:
Week one, Monday: Urmila, Alka and Pia had shared one lunch tin since Class 6. When the class trip was cancelled after someone complained to the principal, a whisper started: "Urmila told."
Week one, Thursday: At lunch, Alka and Pia moved to the window table without a word. Urmila stood holding her tin. In the class chat, someone posted a snake next to her name. She hadn't told anyone anything. That night she lay awake going over every word she'd said that month.
Week three, Tuesday: Urmila finally went to the counsellor, Ms Lobo. "Maybe it's my fault. Maybe I'm just annoying." Ms Lobo said, "When a whole group turns at once, it's rarely about one person. This is not your fault." She asked to speak to the class teacher about the chat that afternoon, and helped Urmila decide who she could sit with tomorrow.

qa.q: Since when had Urmila, Alka and Pia shared a lunch tin?
qa.a: Since Class 6.

qa.q: What was Urmila feeling as she lay awake after Thursday?
qa.a: Urmila felt bewildered and ashamed, going over every word and blaming herself though she had told no one.

qa.q: How did Ms Lobo's response help Urmila?
qa.a: Ms Lobo lifted the blame off Urmila, acted on the chat that same afternoon, and gave her a practical plan for tomorrow's lunch.

qa.q: Why might Alka have moved tables without asking Urmila?
qa.a: Alka may have believed the whisper or feared being linked to the one everyone blamed, so following the group felt safer than asking.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose friends suddenly blame and avoid her, leaving her bewildered, betrayed and blaming herself.

Monday: The hostel's cultural night had flopped. Half the lights failed and the food ran out. By dinner the committee had a culprit. "Joseph was in charge of lights," said Kriti. "Joseph ordered the food," said Amit. Lalremsiami, stirring dal, noticed nobody mentioned the budget being cut in half a week before.
Wednesday: The blame had grown. Now Joseph had "ruined the whole event". Joseph ate in his room. Lalremsiami noticed that Kriti and Amit, who had skipped two planning meetings, were the loudest.
Friday: At the committee meeting, Lalremsiami asked quietly, "Can I ask something? What would we be talking about if we weren't talking about Joseph?"
Silence. Then Neha said, "The budget cut." Amit said, "And, okay, the meetings we skipped." The mood in the room shifted. Someone went to knock on Joseph's door.

qa.q: What had happened to the budget a week before the event?
qa.a: The budget had been cut in half.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling before asking the question on Friday?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt uneasy and suspicious that the blame was too convenient, especially coming loudest from the two who had skipped meetings.

qa.q: Why did Lalremsiami's question work?
qa.a: It didn't defend Joseph or accuse anyone; it simply asked what the blame was covering, so the group named the real causes itself.

qa.q: What was the week like for Joseph?
qa.a: Joseph was likely lonely and ashamed, eating in his room while the whole failure was pinned on him.

grounding: Shows a peer noticing a group's eagerness to blame one person and quietly asking what the blame is helping them avoid.

subtype: Standing up for the blamed person [Response]
passage:
By lunchtime the class had decided, over the long canteen table of a Kolkata college: Jaya had leaked the tutorial answers. "She's always in the professor's cabin," someone said. "Obviously." Heads nodded. Jaya sat at the far end, eating very slowly, not looking up.
Urmila put down her glass. "What's the evidence?"
"Everyone's saying it."
"That's not evidence. The answers came from a photo of the key, right? The key was pinned on the notice board on Monday for ten minutes. Anyone walking past could have taken it." Her voice stayed level. "And Jaya was at the dentist on Monday. She posted about it."
A pause. Tanmay said, "Oh. Yeah, she did."
"I'm not joining this," Urmila said, and moved to sit next to Jaya.
Two others picked up their trays and followed.

qa.q: How long was the answer key pinned on the notice board?
qa.a: For ten minutes on Monday.

qa.q: What does Jaya eating slowly without looking up suggest?
qa.a: Jaya felt hurt, humiliated and alone, wishing to disappear while the table accused her.

qa.q: Which of Urmila's steps broke the spiral?
qa.a: Asking for evidence, calmly laying out the facts, refusing to join, and physically sitting with Jaya, which gave others a way to follow.

qa.q: How might Tanmay see things after Urmila spoke?
qa.a: Tanmay seemed surprised and a bit sheepish, realising he had nodded along without checking 😅

grounding: Shows a peer calmly stating facts, asking for evidence and refusing to join, so one voice breaks a scapegoating spiral.
